archetype.name: Game Manager (veteran bridge starter)
archetype.definition: A big, experienced pocket quarterback who keeps the offense on schedule with quick, short-to-intermediate throws and avoids fumbles, but rarely stretches a defense or wins the money downs on his own.

report.headline: Steady underneath, broken on third down and deep, now listed QB3
report.take:
Brissett is what he has been for a decade: a sturdy, low-variance veteran who gets the ball out, protects it on the ground and lives on the first two levels of the field. The 2026 version leans even harder that way. His time to throw is down 0.28 seconds from last season, his intended air yards sit at 7.75, and his bad-throw rate has improved by 4.2 points. In volume terms he looks like a starter: 214.9 passing yards a game ranks 19th of 47. In efficiency terms he does not. His 5.64 yards per attempt ranks 42nd, his adjusted net yards per dropback is 1.56 below the league average, and his EPA per dropback of -0.075 ranks 34th.

The split that explains the season is depth. Between 10 and 19 air yards he has been very good, +0.509 EPA per attempt over 58 throws with no interceptions, and that band alone produced 29.5 EPA. Everywhere else the offense leaks. Throws behind the line, mostly screens and quick flips that are partly a scheme cost, gave back 17.1 EPA. Deep shots are close to dead: 19.4% completions, -17.6 CPOE and three interceptions on 31 attempts. Short throws are fine but flat at +0.03. He doesn't have the arm-and-anticipation profile to make the defense pay over the top, so the offense has to string together intermediate completions to move, and that is fragile.

The numbers also flatter him in a specific way. With the game within one score he is at -0.21 EPA per play over 191 plays; trailing by nine or more he is at +0.12 with a 5.4 CPOE. A chunk of the yardage came against soft, protecting-the-lead coverage. Third down is the real indictment: -0.445 EPA per play, a 30.1% conversion rate, five of his seven interceptions, and -41.3 EPA on those plays, worse than the whole season's passing total. In the fourth quarter of close games he is at -0.625. Some of that is the protection (Arizona's offense ranks 28th in hit rate allowed), but his pressure-to-sack rate (22.1%, 11th of 38) says he is handling the rush better than in 2025, so the money-down problem is more about decision-making and arm talent than protection.

The trend has turned the evaluation into a moot point for now. Over his last three games his EPA per dropback fell to -0.178 with a -5.8 CPOE and one touchdown on 106 attempts. Week 8 at Dallas was the low point (10 of 23, -14.3 EPA, 58% of the snaps), and as of November 3 he is listed third on the depth chart. Unless something changes above him, his 2026 starting run is over, and what follows describes the player he is if called back in.

strengths.title: Intermediate window is genuinely productive
strengths.body: On throws of 10 to 19 air yards he has a 56.9% completion rate, +3.0 CPOE and no interceptions, adding more EPA than any other area of his game. Those are mostly timing throws in the middle and outside, the kind a veteran reads cleanly in rhythm. His career shows he can live there, and the sample is decent at 58 attempts, so this is a real skill. It also depends heavily on Trey McBride, his most efficient target.

strengths.title: Faster, cleaner pocket operation
strengths.body: He has sped up his release and cut his bad-throw rate from last year, and his pressure-to-sack rate is respectable for a pocket passer. Combined with zero fumbles lost, his sack rate sits below the league average, which matters behind a line that allows a lot of hits. This looks like a deliberate quick-game design, so it should hold whenever he plays.

strengths.title: Efficient under center and on the run
strengths.body: Under center he has seven touchdowns and no interceptions with roughly neutral EPA, and his designed runs (mostly sneaks, by the 1.71 yards per carry) succeed 82.4% of the time. Those are short-yardage and play-action looks where his size and experience help.

concerns.title: Third down and close-game collapse
concerns.body: On third down he converts just 30.1% with five interceptions, and in one-score games his efficiency sinks well below average while it looks fine when trailing big. That is the opposite of what a game manager is supposed to deliver, and it is the main reason the offense stalls. His career has never shown a clutch gear, so expect this to be mostly who he is, though it is unlikely to stay quite this extreme.

concerns.title: No functional deep game
concerns.body: He completes under one in five throws of 20+ air yards with three interceptions and a -17.6 CPOE. That lets defenses squeeze the intermediate area he depends on. His career aDOT has never been high, and this is a long-standing limitation made worse this year.

concerns.title: Falling form and a lost job
concerns.body: His last three games show sharply worse efficiency, and Week 8 ended with him on 58% of the snaps before a depth-chart listing of QB3. The supporting cast is also thinning: Kendrick Bourne is out for the season, Michael Wilson has two broken ribs, and the line is missing a guard. Even if he returns to the field, the conditions are worse than the ones that produced his early-season numbers.

trend.note: He was solid in three of the first five weeks (positive EPA at the Chargers, 49ers and against Detroit), then slid to negative passing EPA in two of the last three, bottoming out at Dallas. A drop to QB3 followed.

nextGame.headline: At Seattle, if he plays at all: the worst possible matchup
nextGame.body:
Seattle is built to beat exactly his profile. The Seahawks rank 3rd in pass defense EPA and 2nd in deep EPA, and they allow the fewest explosive passes in the league, so his already-dead deep game has nowhere to go. They are 3rd in hit rate, against a Cardinals line that already allows a lot of hits. Quarterbacks have managed the fewest yards against them. In Week 2 he threw for 95 yards in a 31-7 loss to them. The one crack is short passing, where Seattle ranks 22nd, which fits his quick game but caps the upside. The Book makes Arizona an 11.5-point underdog, which points to a trailing script where his garbage-time efficiency has looked better.

The bigger issue is availability. He is listed QB3, so the base case is that he does not take meaningful snaps. If he does, he would be without Bourne, likely with a hobbled or absent Michael Wilson, a guard out and a tackle questionable, so even more of the offense would run through McBride. On Seattle's side, edge Uchenna Nwosu was inactive Monday and Leonard Williams left with a stinger. If both miss the game, that would ease the rush somewhat but would not change the coverage problem.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots versus Seattle's shell
keyMatchups.body: His 20+ yard throws are his worst area, and Seattle is among the league's best at taking those away. Expect almost nothing vertical, with interception risk on any forced shot.

keyMatchups.title: Underneath game is the only opening
keyMatchups.body: Seattle ranks 22nd against short passes, which suits his quick release and McBride's role. It is a path to completions and to staying on schedule, not to explosive plays.

keyMatchups.title: Pressure against a depleted line
keyMatchups.body: Seattle hits quarterbacks at the 3rd-highest rate, and Arizona already gives up hits freely, now with Gaines out. In the first meeting he managed only 95 yards.

nextGame.watch: Whether he is active and anywhere above third on the depth chart by Sunday. If he isn't, nothing else here applies.

restOfSeason.body:
The most likely outcome is that he is a backup for the rest of the year, and his snaps depend on injuries or another change at the position above him. If he returns to the lineup, expect the same shape: a high completion rate underneath, a few productive intermediate throws to McBride, little deep, and stalled third downs. With Bourne gone and Wilson hurt, his receiver group gets thinner, which pushes his already-low yards per attempt lower rather than higher. His sack avoidance and zero fumbles are real; his ten touchdowns on a poor red-zone efficiency line are more fragile.

The ranges below assume he starts. Reaching the top of them would take trailing game scripts that inflate attempts, not a return to his 2025 efficiency, which was propped up by a deeper receiving corps.
swingFactors: Whether he regains the starting job or plays only in relief
Michael Wilson's return from fractured ribs
Offensive line health with Gaines and Williams banged up

confidence.note: Full-season sample, but his role is in flux at QB3 and his supporting cast just lost key pieces.
